slides.title: Herding Agents
slides.subtitle: Herdr, an ultrawide, and precise words
slides.notes:
Welcome. This talk covers how I run several AI coding agents at once (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor) without losing track of them, and without them losing track of what I asked for.

Three pieces: Herdr, a terminal workspace manager built for coding agents; a 5120×1440 ultrawide monitor; and precise language in the prompts.

Everything here is written up in two companion articles in this repo (articles/01 and articles/02), and I'll publish them on compositecode.blog.

Refs:
- Herdr: https://herdr.dev
- Blog: https://compositecode.blog/

slides.title:
One agent is a tool.
Six is a zoo.
slides.notes:
Opening tension. One agent is easy to manage: you watch it. Two is a pair. Past three, you're a zookeeper, and somebody has to know which animal is chewing on the fence.

The real cost isn't agents doing the wrong thing. It's agents doing nothing, sitting at a yes/no question for twenty minutes because they don't tap you on the shoulder. Wall-clock time is the most expensive resource in the whole setup.

Pause here. Let it land.

slides.title: A normal Tuesday
slides.notes:
This is the full 5120×1440 ultrawide: one Herdr window, one space (ledger-service), the implementation tab. Two agents side by side, and a diffstat stacked over a shell on the right.

The middle agent is blocked. It's asking me a scoping question. We'll come back to exactly why it stopped; that's the payoff of the second half of the talk.

For now, just notice that everything is on screen at once and nothing is hidden behind a tab.

All screenshots were captured on Herdr 0.8.0 in an isolated named session against throwaway demo repos, with Claude Code in plan mode.

slides.title: Herdr
bullets: Terminal workspace manager for coding agents
One Rust binary, runs in your terminal
Knows when an agent needs you
slides.notes:
What Herdr is, in four lines.

1. It's built for running AI coding agents: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor's agent, Copilot CLI, OpenCode, Devin, and more.
2. A single Rust binary. No Electron. It runs inside iTerm, Ghostty, WezTerm, kitty, Alacritty, even inside tmux.
3. Client/server. A background server owns the terminals; the window is just a client. Close it, drop SSH, and everything keeps running. (While making these screenshots the demo window got closed mid-run; every agent was still there on reattach.)
4. Agent-state detection. That's the point, and it's coming up.

Installing it is the next slide, because it's that short.

Refs:
- https://herdr.dev
- https://herdr.dev/docs/install/
- https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr

slides.title: Installs in one line
slides.notes:
Getting Herdr running is about as short as it gets, which matters, because the barrier to trying a new tool is usually the setup, not the tool.

1. brew install herdr on macOS, or the one-line install script on Linux. It's a single Rust binary: no runtime, no Electron, nothing else to install alongside it.
   Windows note: Herdr runs natively on Windows (x86_64; ARM64 runs it under emulation). Install from PowerShell with powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -c "irm https://herdr.dev/install.ps1 | iex". If endpoint security blocks that, use Command Prompt: curl.exe -fsSLo install.cmd https://herdr.dev/install.cmd && install.cmd && del install.cmd. The installer puts it on your PATH. Windows is generally available but has documented limitations, so check the Windows support page first. Older Windows preview installs stay on the preview channel until you run herdr channel set stable.
2. Run herdr. It starts its background server and attaches you to the default session, inside whatever terminal you already use (iTerm, Ghostty, WezTerm, kitty, Alacritty, even tmux). No config file is required to start.
3. Optional but worth it: herdr integration install claude (or codex, copilot, opencode…) adds a small hook so each agent reports its own state instead of Herdr inferring it from the screen. herdr integration status shows what's wired.

From zero to a working agent workspace in two or three commands. Everything after this in the talk is how I lay it out and how I talk to the agents, not more setup.

Refs:
- https://herdr.dev/docs/install/
- https://herdr.dev/docs/windows-beta/
- https://herdr.dev/docs/quick-start/
- https://herdr.dev/docs/agents/

slides.title: Session › Space › Tab › Pane
slides.notes:
The four nouns, straight from the Herdr concepts page.

- Session: a persistent server namespace. `herdr` attaches to the default; `herdr --session name` gives you an isolated one.
- Workspace (the sidebar calls them spaces): "the top-level project container. Use one workspace per repo, task, or investigation."
- Tab: "a layout inside a workspace."
- Pane: "a real terminal."

If you know tmux, you already have most of this model. The difference is what Herdr knows about what's running in each pane.

Ref: https://herdr.dev/docs/concepts/

slides.title: Blocked. Working. Done. Idle.
slides.notes:
The sidebar. Spaces up top, every agent across every space listed below with a state dot.

- Blocked: needs input, approval, or a decision. This is the one you care about.
- Working: chewing.
- Done: finished, and you haven't looked yet.
- Idle: finished, and you have looked.
- Unknown: Herdr can't tell, usually a plain shell.

This is the shoulder tap agents never gave me.

Tip: run `herdr integration install claude` (or codex, copilot, opencode…) so the agent reports its own lifecycle through a hook instead of Herdr inferring it from the screen. `herdr integration status` shows what's wired.

Refs:
- https://herdr.dev/docs/concepts/
- https://herdr.dev/docs/agents/

slides.title: One space per folder
slides.notes:
Rule one. Every folder I'm actively working in gets a space, named after the folder. Today that's about ten: interlinedlist plus its iOS, macOS, Windows, and Android siblings, an architecture migration, a couple of other projects, and this repo.

Why folders? Because an agent's working directory is the edge of its universe. The space draws the same boundary the agent already lives in, and makes it visible to me.

There's no 'misc' space. Misc is where context goes to die.

My config even sorts the agent list by space: agent_panel_sort = "spaces".

slides.title: Spaces mirror my head
slides.notes:
A second space, transit-tracker, with its own implementation tab. Different folder, different agent, different world.

The sidebar is a direct readout of my working memory. If a folder isn't in it, I'm not working on it. When I'm done with a folder, the space goes away.

This is mostly for my own mental organization. The agents don't care what the sidebar looks like. I do.

Related: when two agents need the same repo at once, each gets a git worktree, which is just another folder, so another space. `herdr worktree create` does it directly.
Ref: https://compositecode.blog/2026/08/19/worktrees/

slides.title: One tab per kind of work
slides.notes:
Rule two. Tabs aren't 'more room.' Tabs are modes, and each one is a different verb.

- domain-modeling: the agent thinks and doesn't type. Plan mode. Glossary and domain notes open beside it.
- implementation: the agent changes code inside an explicit scope, after an approved plan.
- pr-reviews: the agent reads the diff and reports findings. It doesn't fix.

What I'm designing against is verb drift: a reviewer that slides into rewriting the module. The tab is the line it has to cross, drawn on screen.

It also switches my own hat. When I land on a tab called pr-reviews, I'm in review mode before I read a word.

Ref: Ask, Plan, Confirm: https://compositecode.blog/2026/08/20/plan-then-build/

slides.title: domain-modeling
slides.notes:
Domain-modeling tab in ledger-service. One agent column on the left. On the right, the domain notes and the entity code on top, git history below.

The agent was asked to describe a Posting aggregate using only Account, Entry, Journal, Posting, never 'transaction', and not to write code. We'll zoom in on the result later.

The reference panes aren't decoration. They're there so I can check the agent's vocabulary against the agreed vocabulary without switching anything.

slides.title: implementation
slides.notes:
Implementation tab. Two agents, each fenced to a different slice of the code: one planning tests for Posting.Validate, one planning a CLI entrypoint in cmd/main.go only.

On the right, a diffstat over a shell, so I can see what actually changed, not what the agent says changed.

In real work, parallel implementation agents on one repo each get their own worktree and branch.
Ref: https://compositecode.blog/2026/08/19/worktrees/

slides.title: pr-reviews
slides.notes:
PR-reviews tab. Reviewer on the left, raw diff on the right.

Every file:line the reviewer cites can be checked by moving my eyes and nothing else. Trust, but keep the evidence in the same field of view.

The reviewer is read-only. If I want a fix, that's a new, scoped task in the implementation tab.

slides.title:
Tall for agents.
Short for shells.
slides.notes:
Rule three, about panes.

Agents produce long, structured output (plans, findings, tables), so they get full-height vertical splits, side by side: prefix v.

Shells, test runners, git log, and diffstats are glanceable, so they get short horizontal splits stacked in a utility column: prefix minus.

One pane is one agent, one context window, one job. When the job is done, end the conversation. New job, new agent, clean context.

Keys (prefix is ctrl+b): v split vertical, - split horizontal, h/j/k/l move, z zoom, r resize, c new tab, shift+n new space, w space picker, b sidebar, q detach, ? help.
Ref: https://herdr.dev/docs/configuration/

The cheat code. A 5120×1440 ultrawide: two 2560×1440 screens fused, no bezel in the middle.

At normal terminal font sizes that's three or four full-height agent columns, plus a utility column, plus the sidebar, all visible at once.

The next two slides show the same tab at both widths.

slides.title: Half the screen
slides.notes:
The same implementation tab at 2560×1440, a normal 16:9 screen.

Workable. Tight. Two agents and a utility column, and you're already making choices. Add a third agent and you're zooming panes in and out all day.

slides.title: The whole screen
slides.notes:
Same tab on the full ultrawide.

The difference isn't 'more stuff.' It's that nothing is hidden. A blocked agent costs you time silently. Herdr's sidebar tells you THAT something is blocked; having it physically on screen tells you WHY, in peripheral vision, without moving.

The less effort it takes to notice, the shorter the stall.

slides.title: Words are the interface
slides.notes:
Turn. Everything so far is plumbing. The water is language.

A vague word in a chat gets you a vague paragraph. A vague word in an agent prompt gets you a nine-file diff.

I've written about this before:
- Precision in Words, Precision in Code: https://compositecode.blog/2024/12/09/precision-in-words-precision-in-code-the-power-of-writing-in-modern-development/
- AI Prompt Engineering: Mastering Language Constructs: https://compositecode.blog/2025/02/25/ai-prompt-engineering-mastering-language-constructs/

The next three slides are real prompts and real responses from the demo.

slides.title: Use the glossary. Ban the rest.
slides.notes:
Prompt: "Read docs/domain.md and internal/ledger/entry.go. Using only the domain terms Account, Entry, Journal, and Posting (never 'transaction'), describe a Posting aggregate: its invariants, what it owns, and what it must reject. Do not write code."

Accurate language means the same word means the same thing every time: docs, code, prompt, review. That's ubiquitous language from DDD. Agents need it more than people do, because they fill every gap with the statistically likely meaning, which is rarely yours.

'Transaction' is banned because in a ledger it's overloaded: a database transaction, a business event, a statement line.

Result: the model stays inside the vocabulary AND marks which rules it inferred versus which came from the repo.

Refs:
- Notes repos, where the glossary lives: https://compositecode.blog/2026/09/25/notes-repos-as-shared-project-context/
- Fowler, Ubiquitous Language: https://martinfowler.com/bliki/UbiquitousLanguage.html

slides.title: Scope first
slides.notes:
Prompt: "Scope: cmd/main.go only. Plan a minimal CLI entrypoint that loads a Journal from a JSON file and prints the balance per Account. Do not touch internal/ledger. Keep the planned diff under 50 lines."

Scope is the first word. Positive fence, negative fence, size as a number.

The repo had no go.mod, so staying in scope needed a decision. An unfenced agent adds a module, rewires imports, and stubs types in the package I fenced off. This one stopped, went blocked, recommended the in-scope option, and called the other option out of scope.

Herdr flagged it. The ultrawide showed it. One keystroke to answer.

Ref: Hurting or Helping Devs? (scope and diff limits): https://compositecode.blog/2026/04/15/hurting-or-helping-devs/

slides.title: Review means review
slides.notes:
Prompt: "Review the diff main...feature/posting-aggregate. Classify every change as additive, mutative, or destructive. Flag any naming that drifts from docs/domain.md. Report findings as a numbered list with file:line. Do not propose rewrites outside the diff."

Precise verbs: plan, implement, review, and fix are different jobs. Review doesn't mean fix.

Specify the output shape (numbered, file:line) so it can be checked against the diff pane next door.

Because the question was precise, the reviewer had attention to spare. It flagged that any Direction other than exactly "debit" counts as a credit, and that an empty Posting validates as balanced. That's behavioral drift, the quiet kind.

Ref: Additive vs. Mutative vs. Destructive Code Changes: https://compositecode.blog/2026/02/12/additive-vs-mutative-vs-destructive-code-changes-and-why-ai-agents-love-the-wrong-one-at-213am/

slides.title: The prompt shape
slides.notes:
The template I use for Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor alike:

Scope: <paths> only. Do not touch: <paths>.
Context: Read <files / glossary / plan>. Use the terms <A, B, C>; never <overloaded term>.
Task (plan | implement | review): <one sentence, one job>.
Constraints: additive only | under N lines | no new dependencies | tests first.
Output: numbered list | file:line | severity first | test names first.
If anything above is ambiguous or blocks you, stop and ask.

The last line matters most. It turns 'the agent is stuck' from a silent failure into a blocked state, and Herdr turns that into a dot I can see from across the room.

Front-load context instead of looping for it:
- Loop Engineering post: https://compositecode.blog/2026/07/15/loop-engineering-is-mostly-just-broken-sdlc-wearing-a-costume/
- Agent-ready environments: https://compositecode.blog/2026/09/24/agent-ready-local-environments-and-mcp/

slides.title: Ask. Plan. Confirm.
slides.notes:
The gate. No edits until the agent has asked what it needs to ask, shown a plan, and gotten a yes. Approval is scoped to the plan that was approved; if the work grows past it, the agent re-plans.

Backed by tooling: agents start in plan mode (claude --permission-mode plan; Codex and Cursor have their own read-only and ask-first modes).

My side of the loop:
- Blocked: answer in place. If the answer is a decision, write it into the notes repo.
- Done: check the output against the evidence pane. Approve, correct, or open a scoped fix in the implementation tab.
- Job finished: end that conversation.

Ref: https://compositecode.blog/2026/08/20/plan-then-build/

slides.title: Try it
slides.notes:
Getting started takes three lines: install, launch, open help.

Then:
- Make a space per folder you're working in (prefix shift+n, or herdr workspace create --cwd <dir> --label <name>).
- Name tabs for the kind of work (prefix shift+t).
- Agents tall (prefix v), shells short (prefix -).
- herdr integration install claude (and codex, etc.) for accurate state dots.

Worst case, you've got a nice tmux. Best case, you stop finding agents that have been patiently blocked since lunch.

Refs:
- https://herdr.dev/docs/quick-start/
- https://herdr.dev/docs/configuration/
